Turkey, Back from the Sidebar

While everyone was glued to Trump’s “secret deals” with Iran and Lebanon, Turkey quietly walked back into the center of Israel’s strategic picture — and Washington helped roll out the red carpet.

In early July, Ankara will host a full‑scale NATO summit for the first time, with leaders of 32 countries flying in, including Donald Trump and (on the guest list) Volodymyr Zelensky. 

The alliance’s new secretary general, Mark Rutte, is already promising defense contracts worth tens of billions. 

For Turkey, this is more than a diplomatic photo op: it is a staged reminder that a state which buys Russian S‑400s, flirts with Moscow and shields Islamists can still sit at the alliance’s head table and rent out the hall.

On June 24, just before the summit, Washington delivered a very concrete “thank you” package. The State Department notified Congress that it intends to sell Turkey a batch of F110 turbofan engines from General Electric, worth over 700 million dollars. 

These engines are the beating heart of KAAN, Turkey’s flagship indigenous fighter program. Yes, the engines are assembled in Turkey under license — but the export valves are still in U.S. hands. 

Ten units have already been delivered; the talks now circle around another eighty. The message: we control your bottleneck, and we’re willing to loosen it.

There is resistance on the Hill. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, tried to block the deal at the informal stage, pointing to Turkey’s S‑400s and the CAATSA sanctions framework. 

But Congress has just fifteen days to register formal disapproval, both chambers would have to pass a resolution, and Trump can veto it. In that time window, and with this White House, the engines are overwhelmingly likely to go through. 

The “punishment” for S‑400s is melting into a discount for good behavior in the Iran war.

And the engines are just the appetizer. Vice President J.D. Vance has said openly that the administration is reviewing Turkey’s status in the F‑35 program, from which it was kicked out in 2019 after buying the Russian systems. 

The condition, he says, is “necessary legal certifications” — a process run by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Translation: if Ankara plays ball on NATO, Iran and Gaza, the legal paperwork will miraculously discover that the old sins can be forgiven.

Trump, for his part, has gone out of his way to call Erdoğan “a partner” and to tie the thaw directly to Ankara’s decision not to inject itself overtly into the recent U.S.–Iran clash. In this framing, Turkey earns its way back into the good graces of the American defense industry by restraining itself while others fire missiles. The reward arrives as hardware, status and a NATO summit in its capital.

For Israel, this cocktail means the “Turkey file” is no longer a side issue. A Turkey that hosts NATO, buys American engines for a fifth‑generation fighter, and flirts with a return to the F‑35 supply chain is a Turkey that can deepen its reach into Gaza, East Jerusalem, the Eastern Mediterranean and the Arab street with a renewed Atlantic umbrella over its head. 

The same Ankara that courts Hamas and plays lawfare in international forums now gets fresh leverage inside the Western security system — and a friendly White House ready to call that leverage “alliance.”
